messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
- What the failing test sets up:
  - AliasedNamespaceIterationTest.testIterateJDOM delegates to doTestIterate with the JDOM model.
  - The test builds a JXPathContext over a JDOM document that contains two elements in the same namespace URI "ns" but with different prefixes: <a:elem/> and <b:elem xmlns:b="ns"/>.
  - It registers only one prefix in the context: a -> "ns" (createContext registers "a" to "ns").
  - It then asserts that iterating pointers for the XPath /a:doc/a:elem returns two distinct pointers: /a:doc[1]/a:elem[1] and /a:doc[1]/a:elem[2].

- How iteratePointers flows in code:
  - JXPathContextReferenceImpl.iteratePointers(String) immediately delegates to iteratePointers(String, Expression) by compiling the XPath.
  - JXPathContextReferenceImpl.iteratePointers(String, Expression) calls expr.iteratePointers(getEvalContext()).
  - Expression.iteratePointers(EvalContext) computes the result of the expression:
    - If the result is an EvalContext, it is returned as the iterator directly (the usual case for location paths).
    - If the result is a NodeSet, it is converted into a PointerIterator over its pointers.
    - Otherwise, it wraps values into a PointerIterator.

  None of these high-level methods transform the node set in a way that would duplicate one node and drop another on their own; they just expose whatever the lower-level selection logic produced.

- What the bug report observes:
  - For documents where multiple prefixes map to the same namespace URI, iteratePointers returns the first matching element twice and omits the second.
  - This exactly contradicts the test’s expectation that both elements in the same namespace (regardless of prefix) are matched and returned distinctly.

- Where the problem actually occurs:
  - The issue is not in JXPathContextReferenceImpl or Expression.iteratePointers; these simply pass through the results.
  - The fault lies in the name matching and/or positional index calculation used while iterating children for a namespaced name test. Specifically, when determining matches for a step like a:elem (expanded to namespace URI "ns" + local name "elem"), the engine must:
    - Match nodes by namespace URI + local name, not by the prefix string; and
    - Compute the positional index among siblings using namespace URI + local name, not by prefix + local name.

- Why this causes the observed behavior:
  - With two siblings <a:elem/> and <b:elem/>, both are in the same namespace URI and both should match the step a:elem.
  - If the sibling-indexing logic uses the prefix as part of the “same-name” comparison, each prefix starts a separate counting series:
    - The first child <a:elem/> is assigned index [1].
    - The second child <b:elem/> is incorrectly also assigned index [1] because there is no earlier sibling with prefix b, even though there is an earlier sibling in the same namespace with the same local name.
  - When pointers are rendered or de-duplicated using path strings relative to the context’s namespace mapping (which maps the namespace URI to the registered prefix a), both siblings end up represented as /a:doc[1]/a:elem[1].
  - As a result, iteration over pointers yields two entries pointing to what appears to be the first element; effectively, the real second element is lost and the first is seen twice, matching the bug report.

- Conclusion:
  - The root cause is that, somewhere in the node selection/positioning logic (child axis iteration and/or pointer path construction), equality and positional grouping are performed using namespace prefixes instead of namespace URIs. This breaks aliasing (multiple prefixes for the same URI) and leads to duplicate “first element” pointers and omission of the second element for iteratePointers.
  - The fix belongs in the code that:
    - Compares node names during axis iteration, and
    - Computes sibling positions for asPath()/pointer rendering, ensuring comparisons are by namespace URI + local name, not by prefix.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
